direct.title: Interactive System Development Life Cycle Stages

all.title: Interactive System Development Life Cycle Stages

concepts.name: usability
concepts.definition: Usability is an explicit measure of how good a system is from the point of view of the user.

defining_facts.text: Usability is an explicit measure of how good a system is from the point of view of the user.

The International Standards Organization (ISO) 9241-210-2009 standard defines usability as the extent to which a product can be used by specified users to achieve specified goals with effectiveness, efficiency, and satisfaction in a specified context of use.

The three crucial aspects of the International Standards Organization (ISO) 9241-210-2009 usability definition are that a usable product is intended for a specified group of users rather than everybody, that it supports a specified set of goals rather than every conceivable feature, and that it is designed for a specified context of use rather than all usage scenarios.

The three measures of usability are effectiveness, efficiency, and satisfaction; effectiveness is whether the user can do what they want to do, efficiency is how fast the user can do what they want to do, and satisfaction is how satisfied the user is when using the system.

concepts.name: user-centered design
concepts.definition: User-centered design is a design that results from applying a user-centric approach, and it involves users actively or passively in the design or development lifecycle used to build a usable software application.

defining_facts.text: User-centered design is a design that results from applying a user-centric approach, and it involves users actively or passively in the design or development lifecycle used to build a usable software application.
Ben Shneiderman coined the term user-centered design in 1986 in the context of graphical user interfaces.
The objective of user-centered design is to design products that increase usability.

Cooperative design (coined by Greenbaum and Kyng in 1992), participatory design (Schuler and Namioka, 1993), contextual design (Beyer and Holtzblatt, 1997), and human-centered design (the standard term preferred by the International Organization for Standardization (ISO) rather than user-centered design) are related terms that are more or less similar in concept to user-centered design and refer to taking users into the design process.
The user-centered software development approach requires that users be actively or passively involved in the overall software development lifecycle chosen to build a system.

In an Extended Reality (XR) system, interaction design and modeling of user input should follow a user-centered design approach so that the user can provide input data seamlessly, effectively, and easily.

In an Extended Reality (XR) system, perceptual design and modeling of output requires a user-centered design approach because it is crucial to ensure that generated output stimuli match the user's perception of them, so that the user can perceive and understand the output easily.

User-centered design, also called user-centric design, human-centric design, or participatory design, is an approach that actively or passively involves users in the overall design lifecycle, including design and implementation, with the objective of designing application software products that are usable.

User-centered design (UCD), also called user-centric or human-centric design, is a design approach in which the design is based on the user's abilities, context, goals, needs, and expectations, and is ideally driven from the users' point of view rather than by the programmer's convenience.

concepts.name: interface design
concepts.definition: The design-prototype-evaluate loop includes the activities of interface design and interaction design, primarily designing the interface and interaction from the user's point of view based on user requirements, while code design is a separate later design activity.

defining_facts.text: The design-prototype-evaluate loop includes the activities of interface design and interaction design, primarily designing the interface and interaction from the user's point of view based on user requirements, while code design is a separate later design activity.

concepts.name: interactive system development lifecycle
concepts.definition: In the interactive system development lifecycle (ISDLC), building interactive software is broadly similar to building regular software, and the differences are in the requirement gathering, design-prototype-evaluate, and empirical study stages.

defining_facts.text: In the interactive system development lifecycle (ISDLC), building interactive software is broadly similar to building regular software, and the differences are in the requirement gathering, design-prototype-evaluate, and empirical study stages.

The book Human-Computer Interaction, User-Centric Computing for Design discusses the stages of interactive system development life cycles in more detail with respect to broader interactive system development concerns.

The final design of the Majuli virtual reality (VR) tour was developed using the interactive system development lifecycle (ISDL) model, an iterative design-prototype-evaluate cycle that started with a design based on design guidelines and continuously refined design ideas from feedback and observations obtained by involving end users passively or actively.
In the interactive system development lifecycle, empirical evaluation, also called usability evaluation, is the evaluation of the whole system from the point of view of usability.
The interactive system development lifecycle is equally applicable to extended reality (XR) systems.

The interactive system development lifecycle consists of a feasibility study stage, a requirement gathering, analysis and specification stage, a cycle of design, prototyping, and quick evaluation, then code design, coding and implementation, and code testing, and finally an empirical study or usability evaluation stage after the code is bug-free or runs smoothly.

In the interactive system development lifecycle, the design, prototype, and quick evaluation stages form a cycle in which the design is refined based on evaluation results and repeated until the design stabilizes.

Besides the design-prototype-evaluate cycle, the interactive system development lifecycle can have cycles between code design, coding and implementation, and code testing; after empirical usability evaluation, back to the design-prototype-evaluate cycle or interface design; and between the design-prototype-evaluate cycle and requirement gathering.

In the interactive system development lifecycle, cycles should generally be kept infrequent because frequent cycles lead to cost and time overrun, although the design-prototype-evaluate cycle may be frequent.

never_defined.name: interface
never_defined.definition: The key characteristics of a user-centric approach are designing interface elements that are acceptable to users, designing layouts that organize elements on the screen or interface to meet user expectations, helping users perceive the system state from their point of view rather than from technical details, and designing interactions that fulfill users' needs by taking them to desired system states, allowing users to get work done by easily transitioning from one state to a goal state.

never_defined.name: system design
never_defined.definition: Human factors in system design requires designers to know the users' characteristics and design the system accordingly, because users who perform the same broad task, such as a traveler or agent and a database administrator obtaining railway ticket information, can have different expectations, needs, and query-language skills, and therefore require different interfaces for providing input, seeing the outcome, and acting on the outcome.
